title: Atopic Dermatitis in Children
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disease common in African children, often linked with asthma and allergic rhinitis. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria; severity guides treatment. Low‑resource settings require pragmatic use of available investigations and careful monitoring for infection.

sections.p: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a pruritic, chronic inflammatory dermatosis with typical flexural distribution in children. Diagnosis follows the UK Working Party criteria: itchy skin plus three or more of (1) history of flexural rash, (2) personal or family history of atopy, (3) visible dermatitis on the cheeks/forehead or extensor surfaces, (4) dry skin, (5) onset before age 2.
b: Itchy, chronic rash
Flexural or facial distribution
History of asthma, allergic rhinitis, or family atopy

sections.p: Severity is graded using the SCORAD or the simpler POEM score; in low‑resource settings the “mild‑moderate‑severe” clinical categories based on extent (>10% BSA), intensity of erythema, edema, oozing, crusting, and impact on sleep are practical.
b: Mild: <10% BSA, limited sleep disturbance
Moderate: 10‑30% BSA, frequent scratching, sleep loss
Severe: >30% BSA, intense pruritus, secondary infection, sleep deprivation

sections.p: AD results from a combination of skin barrier dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and environmental triggers. In East Africa, common aggravators include house dust mite, pollen, harsh soaps, and frequent use of traditional herbal balms.
b: Filaggrin or other barrier gene mutations
Th2‑dominant immune response
Environmental allergens (dust mite, pollen)
Irritants (detergents, herbal preparations)
Secondary bacterial infection (Staphylococcus aureus)
Co‑existing atopic conditions (asthma, allergic rhinitis)

sections.p: Children present with intense pruritus, erythema, papules, and lichenification in flexural areas (elbows, knees) and on the face/neck. Acute flares show weeping, crusting; chronic disease shows thickened, hyperpigmented plaques. Sleep disturbance is a key functional impact.
b: Itch that worsens at night
Dry, scaly skin
Lichenified plaques in flexures
Possible oozing or crusting in acute flares

sections.p: Investigations are limited; they aim to confirm diagnosis, assess severity, and detect infection.

t.b: Is there secondary infection? Positive culture for Staph aureus guides antibiotic choice
Is there atopic sensitisation? Very high IgE supports atopy but is not required
Identify contact allergens when dermatitis is refractory
Eosinophilia suggests atopic background; normal count does not exclude AD

sections.p: Complications arise from severe inflammation, infection, or systemic effects of chronic disease.
b: Rapidly spreading erythema with fever → cellulitis or sepsis
Crusting with honey‑coloured crusts → impetigo
Persistent sleep loss → growth failure
Signs of allergic sensitisation → anaphylaxis risk with foods

sections.p: Treatment follows a step‑wise approach: restore barrier, control inflammation, treat infection, and address pruritus. Education of caregivers is essential.
b: Emollient therapy: liberal use of fragrance‑free moisturisers, especially after bathing
Topical corticosteroids: low‑potency (hydrocortisone 1%) for mild disease; mid‑potency (betamethasone valerate 0.05%) for moderate‑severe flares
Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus ointment) for steroid‑sparing on face/neck
Antihistamines (diphenhydramine) for night‑time sedation, not primary itch control
Oral antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin) only if bacterial infection is proven or strongly suspected
Education: avoid harsh soaps, keep nails short, use cotton clothing

sections.p: Regular review (every 4‑6 weeks for moderate‑severe disease) monitors control, side‑effects, and infection. Primary prevention focuses on skin barrier maintenance and allergen avoidance.
b: Re‑assess severity with SCORAD/POEM
Reinforce emollient use
Screen for new atopic conditions (asthma, allergic rhinitis)
Vaccinate according to national schedule; consider influenza vaccine

sections.p: Several dermatoses mimic AD, especially in tropical settings.
b: Seborrheic dermatitis – greasy scales on scalp, less pruritic
Scabies – burrows, intense nocturnal itch, often in web spaces
Impetigo – honey‑coloured crusts, bacterial origin
Contact dermatitis – localized to area of irritant exposure

sections.p: Laboratory and clinical findings may be misleading if interpreted without context.
b: Normal IgE does not exclude AD
Mild eosinophilia can be seen in many infections
Negative bacterial culture does not rule out infection if antibiotics were given

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening skin breakdown with pus
Severe sleep deprivation causing daytime somnolence
Signs of anaphylaxis after food exposure

faq.q: Why are emollients the cornerstone of therapy?
faq.a: They restore the defective skin barrier, reduce transepidermal water loss and lower the need for steroids.

faq.q: When should I add a topical calcineurin inhibitor?
faq.a: When the face or neck requires anti‑inflammatory treatment and you want to avoid steroid‑induced atrophy.

faq.q: Is a low‑potency steroid enough for a severe flare?
faq.a: No; moderate‑potency steroids or a short course of higher potency are needed, followed by tapering.

exam: A 2‑year‑old presents with flexural erythema, intense night itch, and a family history of asthma – what diagnostic criteria do you apply and how many must be met? — Use UK Working Party criteria; need itch plus ≥3 of the 5 features.
During a flare the child has honey‑coloured crusts and fever – what is your next step and why? — Obtain a skin swab, start oral antibiotics for suspected impetigo, and continue topical steroids.
You have only petroleum jelly available – how do you incorporate it into the management plan? — Use it as an occlusive emollient after washing; it compensates for lack of specialised moisturisers.

A caregiver reports that the child’s eczema worsened after using a traditional herbal paste – what should you advise? — Explain irritant contact dermatitis, discontinue the paste, and reinforce gentle skin care.
Explain why antihistamines are not first‑line for itch in AD. — They provide sedation but do not address the inflammatory pathway; steroids or calcineurin inhibitors are primary.
What red‑flag sign would prompt urgent referral to a higher‑level centre? — Rapidly spreading cellulitis with systemic signs or signs of sepsis.
How would you differentiate AD from scabies on examination? — Scabies shows burrows in web spaces and linear tracks; AD shows flexural lichenification without burrows.

A child with severe AD is not responding to topical steroids – what systemic options are available in a low‑resource setting? — Consider short courses of oral prednisolone for acute control, then step down; avoid long‑term systemic steroids due to side‑effects.
